items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the unit circle configured in the usual way in the coordinate plane. Suppose a particle [MATH: P] is initially at the point [MATH: (1,0)] and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed angular velocity of [MATH: \dfrac\pi3] radians per second.

Content:
The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0abe58114feee52354b728694995f90d]

Content:
Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as uniform circular motion. This fixed angular velocity is denoted [MATH: \omega,] and we write

Content:
[MATH: \omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.]

Content:
Now, let [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] be the position vector of [MATH: P] at time [MATH: t.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.]

Content:
It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

Content:
- We know that [MATH: \mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j] traces out a unit circle, starting at the point [MATH: (1,0).]
- We can see from the picture that [MATH: P] will return to the starting position after [MATH: t=6] seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is
[MATH: \omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.]
Therefore, we have
[MATH: r(t)|= \cos ((π)/(3) ⋅ t)i + \sin ((π)/(3) ⋅ t)j; = \cos ((πt)/(3))i + \sin ((πt)/(3))j.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: P] indeed returns to its starting location when [MATH: t=6{:}]
[MATH: r(6)|= \cos ((6π)/(3))i + \sin ((6π)/(3))j; = \cos (2π)i + \sin (2π)j; = \cos (0)i + \sin (0)j; = r(0).]

Content:
In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius [MATH: R] centered at [MATH: O] with initial position [MATH: (R,0),] then its position vector [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.]

Content:
Note that for clockwise motion, we have [MATH: \omega < 0.]

Content:
Let's see an example.

items.title: Finding the Position Function of an Object Moving With Circular Motion

sections.normalized_html: A particle moves along a clockwise circular path with center [MATH: O] in the [MATH: xy]-plane with a constant angular velocity of [MATH: 3 \textrm{ rad/s}.] Given that the object is at the position [MATH: (7,0)] when [MATH: t=0,] find the position function of the particle.
sections.readable_text: A particle moves along a clockwise circular path with center [MATH: O] in the [MATH: xy]-plane with a constant angular velocity of [MATH: 3 \textrm{ rad/s}.] Given that the object is at the position [MATH: (7,0)] when [MATH: t=0,] find the position function of the particle.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius [MATH: R] in the [MATH: xy]-plane with a constant angular velocity [MATH: \omega] is given by [MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos \omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin \omega t \,\mathbf j\right),] where it is assumed that the circle is centered at [MATH: O,] and particle is at the position [MATH: (R,0)] when [MATH: t=0.]

Since the object's initial position is [MATH: (7,0),] we have that [MATH: \mathbf r(0)=\,7\mathbf i,] and we can conclude that the radius of the circle [MATH: R=7.]

Therefore, since we have [MATH: R=7] and [MATH: \omega= -3 \textrm{ rad/s}] (negative because the motion is clockwise), we get that the position function is given by

[MATH: r(t)|= 7(\cos (− 3t)i + \sin (− 3t)j); = 7(\cos 3ti − \sin 3tj).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose a particle [MATH: P] moves along a circle of radius [MATH: R] centered at the origin in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c27af17f21411b341412bce84aa2b593]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The position vector [MATH: \mathbf r] extends from the origin to [MATH: P] in the radial direction, while
- the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf v] points in the direction of the particle's motion, tangential to the circle.

Content:
First, let's assume that [MATH: P] is at the point [MATH: (R,0)] when [MATH: t=0.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).]

Content:
We can easily derive a convenient formula relating [MATH: \mathbf v] and [MATH: \omega] by differentiating [MATH: \mathbf r(t){:}]

Content:
Differentiating once, we get
[MATH: v(t)|= r^{′}(t); = (R(\cos ωti + \sin ωtj))^{′}; = Rω(− \sin ωti + \cos ωtj).]
By computing the magnitude of this vector, we see that
[MATH: ||v||^{2}|= R^{2}ω^{2}((− \sin ωt)^{2} + (\cos ωt)^{2}); = R^{2}ω^{2}(\sin^{2} ωt + \cos^{2} ωt); = R^{2}ω^{2}.]
Taking the square root, we get
[MATH: ||\mathbf v || = R|\omega|.]

Content:
Note that while the magnitude of the velocity vector (i.e., the speed) is constant, its direction is continuously changing, which means that an object in uniform circular motion also experiences acceleration (more on this shortly).

sections.normalized_html: An object moves along a circular path with position [MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= 5\cos \pi t \, \mathbf i + 5\sin \pi t \,\mathbf j] meters. Find the speed of the object at time [MATH: t,] measured in seconds.
sections.readable_text: An object moves along a circular path with position [MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= 5\cos \pi t \, \mathbf i + 5\sin \pi t \,\mathbf j] meters. Find the speed of the object at time [MATH: t,] measured in seconds.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Method 1

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get [MATH: v(t)|= (r(t))^{′}; = (5\cos πti + 5\sin πtj)^{′}; = − 5π\sin πti + 5π\cos πtj.]

To find the speed, we calculate the magnitude of the velocity vector as follows: [MATH: ||v(t)|||= sqrt((− 5π\sin πt)^{2} + (5π\cos πt)^{2}); = sqrt(25π^{2}\sin^{2} πt + 25π^{2}\cos^{2} πt); = sqrt(25π^{2}(\sin^{2} πt + \cos^{2} πt)); = 5π]

Therefore, the object's speed is [MATH: 5 \pi \textrm{ m/s}.]

Note that the speed is constant, but the velocity is not.

Method 2

For uniform circular motion in the [MATH: xy]-plane, we have

[MATH: ||\mathbf v|| = R|\omega|,] where [MATH: R] is the radius of the circle, and [MATH: \omega] is the angular velocity.

In our case, the radius of the circle is [MATH: R=5\,\textrm m] and the angular frequency [MATH: \omega = \pi \,\textrm{rad/s}.] Therefore,

[MATH: ||\mathbf v|| = 5\cdot |\pi| = 5\pi \textrm{ m/s}.]

Content:
Let's return to our particle [MATH: P] moving along a circle of radius [MATH: R] centered at the origin in the [MATH: xy] plane.

Content:
Once again, let's assume that [MATH: P] is at the point [MATH: (R,0)] when [MATH: t=0.] Then, we have

Content:

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf v(t) =R\omega\left(-\sin\omega t \, \mathbf i + \cos\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)]

Content:
Differentiating once more, we get an expression for the acceleration vector:

Content:
[MATH: a(t)|= v^{′}(t); = Rω(− \sin ωti + \cos ωtj)^{′}; = Rω(− ω\cos ωti − ω\sin ωtj); = − ω^{2} ⋅ R(\cos ωti + \sin ωtj); = − ω^{2}r]

Content:
To summarize,

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf a = -\omega^2 \mathbf r.]

Content:
Therefore, the acceleration vector acts in the opposite direction to [MATH: \mathbf r.] In other words, [MATH: \mathbf a] points toward the center of the circle. Moreover, we have

Content:
[MATH: ||\mathbf a|| = \omega^2 || \mathbf r ||.]

sections.normalized_html:
Method 1

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get [MATH: v(t)|= (r(t))^{′}; = (4(\cos 3ti + \sin 3tj))^{′}; = − 12\sin 3ti + 12\cos 3tj.]

Then, we find the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector. [MATH: a(t)|= (v(t))^{′}; = (− 12\sin 3ti + 12\cos 3tj)^{′}; = − 36\cos 3ti − 36\sin 3tj]

Finally, we calculate the magnitude of the acceleration as follows: [MATH: ||a(t)|||= sqrt((− 36\cos 3t)^{2} + (− 36\sin 3t)^{2}); = sqrt(36^{2}\cos^{2} 3t + 36^{2}\sin^{2} 3t); = sqrt(36^{2}); = 36]

Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is [MATH: 36\, \textrm{m/s}^2.]

Note that [MATH: ||\mathbf a||] is constant, but [MATH: \mathbf a] is not.

Method 2

For uniform circular motion in the [MATH: xy]-plane, we have

[MATH: \mathbf a = -\omega^2\mathbf r \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad ||\mathbf a|| = \omega^2||\mathbf r||.]

In our case, the radius of the circle is [MATH: a=4\,\textrm m] and the angular frequency [MATH: \omega = 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.] Therefore,

[MATH: ||\mathbf a|| = 3^2\cdot |4| = 36\, \textrm{m/s}^2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the unit circle configured in the usual way in the coordinate plane. Suppose a particle [MATH: P] is initially at the point [MATH: (1,0)] and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed angular velocity of [MATH: \dfrac\pi3] radians per second.

Content:
The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0abe58114feee52354b728694995f90d]

Content:
Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as uniform circular motion. This fixed angular velocity is denoted [MATH: \omega,] and we write

Content:
[MATH: \omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.]

Content:
Now, let [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] be the position vector of [MATH: P] at time [MATH: t.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.]

Content:
It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

Content:
- We know that [MATH: \mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j] traces out a unit circle, starting at the point [MATH: (1,0).]
- We can see from the picture that [MATH: P] will return to the starting position after [MATH: t=6] seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is
[MATH: \omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.]
Therefore, we have
[MATH: r(t)|= \cos ((π)/(3) ⋅ t)i + \sin ((π)/(3) ⋅ t)j; = \cos ((πt)/(3))i + \sin ((πt)/(3))j.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: P] indeed returns to its starting location when [MATH: t=6{:}]
[MATH: r(6)|= \cos ((6π)/(3))i + \sin ((6π)/(3))j; = \cos (2π)i + \sin (2π)j; = \cos (0)i + \sin (0)j; = r(0).]

Content:
In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius [MATH: R] centered at [MATH: O] with initial position [MATH: (R,0),] then its position vector [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.]

Content:
Note that for clockwise motion, we have [MATH: \omega < 0.]

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Position Function of an Object Moving With Circular Motion

Example Prompt:
A particle moves along a clockwise circular path with center [MATH: O] in the [MATH: xy]-plane with a constant angular velocity of [MATH: 3 \textrm{ rad/s}.] Given that the object is at the position [MATH: (7,0)] when [MATH: t=0,] find the position function of the particle.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius [MATH: R] in the [MATH: xy]-plane with a constant angular velocity [MATH: \omega] is given by
[MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos \omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin \omega t \,\mathbf j\right),]
where it is assumed that the circle is centered at [MATH: O,] and particle is at the position [MATH: (R,0)] when [MATH: t=0.]

Since the object's initial position is [MATH: (7,0),] we have that [MATH: \mathbf r(0)=\,7\mathbf i,] and we can conclude that the radius of the circle [MATH: R=7.]

Therefore, since we have [MATH: R=7] and [MATH: \omega= -3 \textrm{ rad/s}] (negative because the motion is clockwise), we get that the position function is given by

[MATH: r(t)|= 7(\cos (− 3t)i + \sin (− 3t)j); = 7(\cos 3ti − \sin 3tj).]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Linear vs. Angular Velocity

Content:
Suppose a particle [MATH: P] moves along a circle of radius [MATH: R] centered at the origin in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c27af17f21411b341412bce84aa2b593]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The position vector [MATH: \mathbf r] extends from the origin to [MATH: P] in the radial direction, while
- the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf v] points in the direction of the particle's motion, tangential to the circle.

Content:
First, let's assume that [MATH: P] is at the point [MATH: (R,0)] when [MATH: t=0.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).]

Content:
We can easily derive a convenient formula relating [MATH: \mathbf v] and [MATH: \omega] by differentiating [MATH: \mathbf r(t){:}]

Content:
Differentiating once, we get
[MATH: v(t)|= r^{′}(t); = (R(\cos ωti + \sin ωtj))^{′}; = Rω(− \sin ωti + \cos ωtj).]
By computing the magnitude of this vector, we see that
[MATH: ||v||^{2}|= R^{2}ω^{2}((− \sin ωt)^{2} + (\cos ωt)^{2}); = R^{2}ω^{2}(\sin^{2} ωt + \cos^{2} ωt); = R^{2}ω^{2}.]
Taking the square root, we get
[MATH: ||\mathbf v || = R|\omega|.]

Content:
Note that while the magnitude of the velocity vector (i.e., the speed) is constant, its direction is continuously changing, which means that an object in uniform circular motion also experiences acceleration (more on this shortly).

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Velocity and Speed of a Particle Moving With Circular Motion

Example Prompt:
An object moves along a circular path with position [MATH: \mathbf {r}(t)= 5\cos \pi t \, \mathbf i + 5\sin \pi t \,\mathbf j] meters. Find the speed of the object at time [MATH: t,] measured in seconds.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Method 1

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get
[MATH: v(t)|= (r(t))^{′}; = (5\cos πti + 5\sin πtj)^{′}; = − 5π\sin πti + 5π\cos πtj.]

To find the speed, we calculate the magnitude of the velocity vector as follows:
[MATH: ||v(t)|||= sqrt((− 5π\sin πt)^{2} + (5π\cos πt)^{2}); = sqrt(25π^{2}\sin^{2} πt + 25π^{2}\cos^{2} πt); = sqrt(25π^{2}(\sin^{2} πt + \cos^{2} πt)); = 5π]

Therefore, the object's speed is [MATH: 5 \pi \textrm{ m/s}.]

Note that the speed is constant, but the velocity is not.

Method 2

For uniform circular motion in the [MATH: xy]-plane, we have

[MATH: ||\mathbf v|| = R|\omega|,]
where [MATH: R] is the radius of the circle, and [MATH: \omega] is the angular velocity.

In our case, the radius of the circle is [MATH: R=5\,\textrm m] and the angular frequency [MATH: \omega = \pi \,\textrm{rad/s}.] Therefore,

[MATH: ||\mathbf v|| = 5\cdot |\pi| = 5\pi \textrm{ m/s}.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Acceleration Vector

Content:
